hook_clip: My spec would have emailed everyone about laptops they've had for years.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of Asset Panda a small company needs for laptops, monitors and phones. A register with a tag on every item. Check-out and check-in, so every item has one holder and a full history. Warranty reminders. And an asset check, where everyone confirms what they hold.

The core rule is one holder. An item has a holder only while it's assigned. Moving it from Jo to Maya is a check-in, then a check-out, so the history shows both. And nobody can be deactivated while they still hold company equipment. The app lists what to collect first.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation and the register. Check-out, check-in and statuses. Warranty and asset checks. Then import and export. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser.

Here's what it built. The items screen shows eight items, worth nine thousand and fifty-three dollars, and one warranty ending soon. The Dell monitor went from Jo to Maya, and the history shows both rows. The daily job logged two warranty reminders and Priya's check-out email. In the asset check, Jo confirmed one item and disputed the other. The import preview refused a duplicate serial and an unknown holder. And on a phone, Jo answers the asset check.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all twenty-one checks passed, along with one hundred and sixteen automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed eighty-two places where Claude had to guess. An import sent a you now have email for every row, even for equipment people already had. Nothing said whether a lost laptop still blocks someone's deactivation. And the found-item page was only defined for signed-in staff. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't production-ready. Production sign-in, real email delivery, a hosted scheduler, hosting and printed labels were never tested. Check those yourself before your team relies on it.

So is it worth building? Asset Panda doesn't publish prices. Its pricing page asks for your details for a custom quote, with a free seven-day trial. Build it if you track laptops in a spreadsheet that's never quite true, and nobody knows what to collect when someone leaves. Buy it if you track thousands of assets across sites, or need inspections and maintenance schedules.
Everything is in one file. The data model, thirteen rules, the seed data, four phase prompts and twenty-one checks, with all eighty-two fixes included.
